name: Search Quality Evaluation
intent: Decide whether a ranking change made search better by scoring both rankers against a fixed set of judged queries with precision, recall and NDCG, and by confirming with an online experiment, instead of trusting a few examples.
scenario: A team has a candidate ranker B and wants to replace the current ranker A. Six queries have been judged: documents graded 0 (irrelevant) to 3 (perfect). Three are head queries that make up 80% of traffic ("iphone case", "laptop", "headphones") and three are rare tail queries ("gift for dad who likes coffee"). Averaged over all six queries, B wins on NDCG@5, 0.66 against 0.60. Weighted by traffic, A wins, 0.82 against 0.70. Drop one query and the winner changes again. The team must decide which result to believe.
problem: Search quality is easy to feel and hard to measure. A developer tries five queries, likes what B returns, and ships it; a week later head-query clicks have fallen. Every ranking change helps some queries and hurts others, so one number is only as meaningful as the queries behind it and the weights between them. Clicks seem like a free signal, but people click what is shown first, and a click is not a judgment that the result was good. Without a repeatable measure the team cannot tell progress from noise, or catch a regression before users do.

howItWorks.title: Build a judged set
howItWorks.text: A judged set is a list of (query, document, grade) triples. The queries should be sampled from real traffic, including the long tail. Raters (or, carefully, a model checked against raters) give each document a grade such as 0 irrelevant, 1 marginal, 2 good, 3 perfect, following written guidelines so two raters agree. The set is fixed, so rerunning a ranker on it gives a comparable number. Unjudged documents are usually treated as irrelevant, which quietly penalizes a ranker that finds good documents nobody graded.

howItWorks.title: Precision and recall at k
howItWorks.text: Take the top k results of a ranker and call a document relevant if its grade is 1 or more. Precision@k is the share of those k results that are relevant: 2 of 3 is 0.67. Recall@k is the share of all relevant documents for the query that appear in the top k: if 4 documents are relevant and 3 are in the top 5, recall@5 is 0.75. Precision tells you how much of what the user sees is useful; recall tells you how much of the useful material was found. Both ignore the order inside the top k, and neither uses the grades beyond relevant or not.

howItWorks.title: NDCG: grades and position
howItWorks.text: Normalized discounted cumulative gain scores the order. In the widely used form (the one in this example), each result gives a gain of 2^grade - 1 (so a grade 3 is worth 7 and a grade 1 is worth 1; the original definition uses the grade itself, which rewards top grades less steeply), discounted by log2 of its position plus one, so a perfect document at position 1 counts fully and the same document at position 5 counts much less. DCG is the sum over the top k. Dividing by the DCG of the ideal ordering gives NDCG between 0 and 1, comparable across queries. In the example, ranker A has NDCG@5 of 0.96 on "iphone case" and 0.00 on the coffee query.

howItWorks.title: Averages depend on which queries count, and how much
howItWorks.text: The headline number is a weighted average over queries, and the weights are a choice. Counting every query equally treats a query searched once a month like one searched a million times. Weighting by traffic matches what users experience but makes the tail invisible. With the example data B wins by 0.06 with equal weights and loses by 0.12 with traffic weights; on tail queries alone B leads 0.63 to 0.25, and on head queries alone A leads 0.97 to 0.71. A single query with a 0 against a 1.00 moves a six-query average by 0.17, which is why six queries cannot settle anything: use hundreds, look at the per-query wins and losses, and run a paired significance test or a bootstrap on the differences.

howItWorks.title: Offline metrics, clicks and A/B tests
howItWorks.text: Offline metrics are fast, cheap and repeatable, so they filter ideas, but they measure what raters judged, not what users do. Click-through is a real user signal and a noisy one: higher results get more clicks whatever their quality (position bias), a click can be a mistake, and a quick return to the results can mean the result was bad. Treat it as evidence, not truth. The deciding step for a change that looks good offline is an online experiment: send a share of users to B and compare behavior that matters (queries abandoned, reformulations, purchases, time to a successful click) with A, long enough to be statistically sound. Offline metrics guide, online tests decide.

pros: A fixed judged set gives a repeatable number, so every change can be checked in minutes
NDCG uses graded relevance and position, which matches how people read a result list
Per-query results show who a change helps and who it hurts, not just the average
A regression suite of judged queries catches a bad ranking change before release
cons: Judging is slow and costly, and raters disagree, so the set is small and imperfect
A small set gives noisy averages: one query can swing the result
Judgments go stale as products, language and intent change
Offline gains do not always appear online, and the reverse
whenToUse: Any change to analyzers, field weights, BM25 parameters, synonyms or a learned ranker
Comparing a new ranking model with the current one before an experiment
Monitoring search quality over time with a fixed set of important queries
whenNotToUse: As the only gate for shipping: confirm with an online experiment on real users
Queries that have no stable right answer, where raters cannot agree on a grade
Judging a ranker on queries it was tuned on, which measures memorization, not quality
pitfalls: Deciding from a handful of favorite queries, which is anecdote, not evidence
Reporting one average without the query mix: head and tail queries can point in opposite directions
Tuning k1, b or a model against the judged set until it scores well, then testing on the same queries
Treating unjudged results as irrelevant, which punishes a ranker for finding documents nobody graded
Reading clicks as relevance: position bias and mistaken clicks make them a noisy signal
Ignoring statistical noise: a difference of 0.02 on 20 queries is usually not a difference

roles.label: Relevance rater
roles.description: Grades documents for a query from 0 to 3, following written guidelines.

roles.label: Judged set
roles.description: The fixed list of queries, documents and grades that every ranker is scored on.

roles.label: Ranker
roles.description: The current ranker A or the candidate B, each returning a ranked list per query.

roles.label: Metric job
roles.description: Computes precision, recall and NDCG per query and averages them with chosen weights.

roles.label: A/B experiment
roles.description: Serves each ranker to a share of real users and measures their behavior.

quiz.question: A developer tries 5 favorite queries, finds that the new ranker looks better on all of them, and ships it. Head-query clicks then fall. What was the main mistake?
options: The new ranker should have been tested with a higher k.
Five hand-picked queries are an anecdote that may not represent traffic, while a judged, sampled set would show the head-query loss.
Clicks cannot be measured after a launch, so the fall is a measurement error.
Rankers must always be shipped to tail queries first.
quiz.explanation: Favorite queries are not a sample of traffic, and tail queries that impress can hide losses on the head queries that carry most searches. A sampled judged set, weighted by traffic and looked at per query, would have shown it. Clicks can be measured, and nothing requires a tail-first launch.

quiz.question: On a set of 6 judged queries, ranker B beats A by 0.06 NDCG on average. Removing one query makes A the winner. What does this show?
options: One query was large enough to decide the average, so the set is too small to trust the comparison.
The NDCG formula is wrong whenever a query is left out.
Ranker B must have been tuned on that query.
Averages should never be used to compare rankers.
quiz.explanation: With 6 queries each one carries about 17% of the average, so a query where A scores 0.00 and B scores 1.00 can decide the winner. The remedy is more queries, a look at per-query wins, and a significance test. Averages are fine when the set is large enough, and nothing says B was tuned on that query.

quiz.question: Ranker B wins on every metric offline. Why still run an A/B test before replacing A?
options: The offline metrics cannot be computed for a production system.
Offline metrics are only valid for the first 10 results.
Judged queries and grades only approximate what users want, so real behavior must confirm the gain.
An A/B test is required by law for search changes.
quiz.explanation: Offline numbers measure agreement with raters on a fixed set of queries. They guide the choice but cannot replace measuring what real users do (reformulations, abandoned searches, purchases). The other statements are false: offline metrics are computed on production data all the time, they apply to any k, and no law requires such tests.
